# Abstract

This study reconstructs the historical population and settlement geography of Outer Mongolia across seven centuries from the coronation of Temüjin as Chinggis Khan in 1206AD to the collapse of the Qing dynasty and the establishment of the Bogd Khanate in 1912AD under JADE. Covering 1.562.476 km² (26.461 five-arcminute grid cells) partitioned into six historical administrative territories (the four Khalkha aimags of Tüsheet Khan, Setsen Khan, Sain Noyon Khan and Zasagt Khan, together with the western Khovd frontier ambanship and the Khövsgöl-Dariganga border tracts), the demographic aggregate grew from a pastoral baseline of 700k (700.000) in 1206AD to an imperial peak of 780k (780.000) in 1290AD under Khubilai Khan [@wusongdi2000zhongguo; @allsen1987mongol; @atwood2004encyclopedia]. Following the collapse of the Yuan dynasty in 1368AD and Ming retaliatory campaigns across the steppe, population receded to 680k (680.000) in 1368AD and trough of 580k (580.000) by 1450AD amidst Northern Yuan factional fragmentation [@cao2024population; @bawden1989modern]. A sixteen-century resurgence under Dayan Khan carried the total to 610k in 1550AD before the destructive Dzungar-Khalkha wars of 1688AD drove numbers down to a modern nadir of 560k (560.000) in 1700AD [@dicosmo1998qing; @caoshuji2001zhongguo]. Qing administrative reorganisation following the 1691AD Dolon Nor assembly stabilised frontier pastoralism, and eighteenth-century monastic urbanisation around Ikh Khüree (Urga) and banner administrative headquarters lifted the aggregate to 610k in 1776AD, 625k in 1820AD, 636.700 in 1900AD and 644k (644.000) at national independence in 1912AD [@caoshuji2001zhongguo; @pozdneyev1971mongolia; @maiskii1921sovremennaya]. Intra-regional density surfaces are calibrated through Paciorek-Schervish non-stationary Matérn ($\nu = 3/2$) kriging across 87.810 East Asian archaeological site records and 1.274 domestic catchments ($\tau_1 = 1,50$, effective short range 73,43 km, regularised nugget-to-sill 0,04, WLS $R^2 = 0,9995$) harmonised with 254 catalogued settlements [@paciorek2006spatial; @Bemmann2020Karakorum].

# Background

## The Ecological and Steppe Demographic Baseline

The demographic carrying capacity of the Mongolian plateau has historically been circumscribed by extreme continental climate, arid grassland ecology and high seasonal vulnerability to winter freezes (*dzud*) [@DR2019Modeling; @Struck2022Central]. Across 1,562M km² extending from the Altai Mountains in the west to the Kherlen and Menen steppes in the east, semi-arid steppe and forest-steppe biomes supported mobile pastoral nomadic production focused on the five traditional herds: horses, sheep, goats, cattle and Bactrian camels [@Y2026Following; @M2025Bioavailable].

Sedentary agricultural production was confined to narrow river valleys along the Orkhon, Tuul, Selenge and Kherlen drainage basins, where localized irrigation canals sustained mediaeval agronomy and military supply bases [@Tolnai2026Tracing; @Wright2025Zuun]. Prior to imperial unification, pastoral human density rarely exceeded 0,45 persons per km², with mobile encampments (*khuree* and *ail*) circulating seasonally between upland summer pastures (*zuslan*) and sheltered lowland winter camps (*öwoljoo*) [@DR2019Modeling; @Honichud2022Mongolian].

## Chinggisid Imperial Consolidation and Decimal Mobilisation (1206 to 1368AD)

The kurultai of 1206AD along the Onon River transformed Mongolian society by replacing fragmented tribal confederations with a unified decimal administrative-military structure [@atwood2004encyclopedia; @allsen1987mongol]. Chinggis Khan partitioned the nomadic population into tens (*arban*), hundreds (*jaghun*), thousands (*mingghan*) and ten-thousands (*tümen*), binding pastoral lineages directly to imperial state service and breaking ancestral clan exclusivity [@Honichud2022Mongolian; @A2026Genomes].

The *Secret History of the Mongols* records ninety-five original *mingghan* commanders in 1206AD, representing approximately 95.000 adult male warriors fit for military service [@allsen1987mongol; @wusongdi2000zhongguo]. Applying standard pastoral household dependency multipliers of 6,5 to 7,5 persons per mounted trooper indicates an imperial core population of roughly 650k to 720k nomads across the Mongolian homeland in 1206AD, harmonising precisely with the module baseline total of 700k (700.000) [@wusongdi2000zhongguo; @cao2024population].

Decimal censuses executed under Great Khans Ögedei (1235–1236AD) and Möngke (1252–1259AD) systematically registered taxable households and pastoral herds across Mongolia and northern China [@allsen1987mongol]. The establishment of the imperial postal relay system (*örtoo* or *yam*) created fixed logistical corridors linking the steppe heartland to Central Asia, Persia and China, encouraging early roadside settlement nuclei and artisan depots [@Franklin2023Archaeology; @Vasyutin2026Origins]. During the reign of Khubilai Khan, Yuan fiscal compendia and Songdi Wu's demographic syntheses place the population of the Mongolian plateau at 780k in 1290AD, representing the mediaeval demographic zenith of the Chinggisid homeland [@wusongdi2000zhongguo; @cao2024population].

## Karakorum and Avraga Urbanism in a Pastoral Nomad Society

Early Chinggisid statecraft produced an extraordinary urban experiment: the creation of fixed imperial administrative capitals inside an exclusively pastoral nomadic society [@Bemmann2020Karakorum; @Vasyutin2026Origins]. The earliest Chinggisid headquarters was Avraga Ord along the upper Kherlen River in eastern Mongolia, which served as Chinggis Khan's principal seasonal base camp and state ritual locus from 1200AD to approximately 1220AD [@Wright2025Zuun; @Anon2021Study]. Archaeological excavations at Avraga demonstrate extensive metallurgical workshops, craft production, iron casting and monumental earthen platforms supporting imperial pavilions, housing an estimated peak population of 14k inhabitants around 1210AD [@Wright2025Zuun; @Bemmann2020Karakorum].

In 1235AD, Ögedei Khan founded the permanent walled capital of Karakorum (*Qara Qorum*) in the Orkhon River valley, enclosing 1,8 km² within earthen ramparts flanked by the monumental Wan'an Gong palace [@Bemmann2020Karakorum; @Tolnai2026Tracing]. As documented by Franciscan envoy William of Rubruck in 1254AD, Karakorum was divided into distinct commercial and metallurgical quarters: a Muslim mercantile precinct, a Chinese artisan quarter with iron foundries and ceramic kilns, Christian churches, Daoist temples and Buddhist shrines, surrounding the silver tree fountain sculpted by Parisian goldsmith Guillaume Boucher [@Bemmann2020Karakorum; @Franklin2023Archaeology].

Karakorum reached an urban peak of 38k inhabitants in 1255AD, sustained by massive grain imports transported up the Orkhon River and grain produced in state-managed agricultural colonies along the Orkhon and Tuul valleys [@Tolnai2026Tracing; @wusongdi2000zhongguo]. When Khubilai Khan transferred the primary imperial seat southward to Shangdu and Dadu (Beijing) in 1264AD, Karakorum retained prestige as the northern administrative capital of the Lingbei Branch Secretariat (*Lingbei xingsheng*), but its civilian population gradually contracted until Ming military incursions razed the fortifications in 1380AD [@Bemmann2020Karakorum; @cao2024population].

## Northern Yuan Fragmentation and the Six Tümen of Dayan Khan

The expulsion of the Yuan court from Beijing by the Ming dynasty in 1368AD forced Toghon Temür and the imperial remnants back into the Mongolian steppe, inaugurating the Northern Yuan period (1368 to 1635AD) [@bawden1989modern; @atwood2004encyclopedia]. Imperial authority disintegrated into chronic civil conflict between the eastern Chinggisid Mongols and the western Oirat confederation [@bawden1989modern]. Steppe warfare, retaliatory Ming campaigns led by the Yongle Emperor across the Kherlen and Tuul rivers, and disruptions to trans-Eurasian trade routes reduced regional population from 680k in 1368AD to 580k by 1450AD [@cao2024population; @dicosmo1998qing].

Demographic and political recovery began under Batumöngke Dayan Khan (1479–1517AD) and Queen Mandukhai Khatun, who reunited the eastern Mongols under the Six Tümen (*Zurgaan Tümen*) system [@bawden1989modern; @atwood2004encyclopedia]. The Six Tümen divided eastern Mongolia into the Three Left Wings (Khalkha, Chahar and Uriankhai) and the Three Right Wings (Ordos, Tümed and Yöngshiyebü) [@bawden1989modern].

The Northern Khalkha, occupying the ancestral valleys of the Kherlen, Tuul, Orkhon and Selenge rivers, were allocated to Dayan Khan's youngest son G Gersenz Jalayir Khongtaiji [@bawden1989modern]. Gersenz partitioned the Khalkha heartland among his seven sons, creating the genealogical foundations of the four great Khalkha aimags: Tüsheet Khan in the central valleys, Setsen Khan in the east, Zasagt Khan in the west, and later Sain Noyon Khan carved from western Tüsheet lands [@bawden1989modern; @atwood2004encyclopedia]. Dayan Khan's institutional stabilisation fostered demographic recovery, lifting regional population to 610k by 1550AD [@cao2024population].

## Gelugpa Monasticism, Zanabazar and the Rise of Ikh Khüree

The late sixteenth century witnessed the second conversion of Mongolia to Tibetan Buddhism, fundamentally altering settlement geography and demography [@bawden1989modern; @Ujeed2015Establishment]. In 1578AD, Altan Khan of the Tümed met Sonam Gyatso, the third hierarch of the Gelugpa order, bestowing the title *Dalai Lama* [@bawden1989modern; @nrsaikhan2025Buddhist].

Inspired by this alliance, Abtai Sain Khan of the Khalkha visited the Dalai Lama and in 1586AD established Erdene Zuu monastery immediately adjacent to the ruins of Karakorum in the Orkhon valley, constructing one hundred and eight stupas around three monumental Chinese-style temples [@Bemmann2020Karakorum; @bawden1989modern]. Erdene Zuu served as the spiritual and symbolic heart of Khalkha Buddhism, re-anchoring nomadic demographic gravity to the Orkhon basin.

The consolidation of the Buddhist church culminated in the recognition of Zanabazar (Öndör Gegeen, 1635–1723AD), son of Tüsheet Khan Gombodorj, as the first Bogd Gegeen or Jebtsundamba Khutuktu [@bawden1989modern; @Seddon2009Writings]. In 1639AD, an assembly of Khalkha nobles at Shireet Tsagaan Nuur founded a movable palace-monastery (*Örgöö*) for the young spiritual leader [@bawden1989modern].

This mobile religious encampment, known successively as Örgöö, Da Khüree and Ikh Khüree (Urga), migrated twenty-eight times across central Mongolia before permanently settling at its present site in the Tuul River basin beneath the sacred peak of Bogd Khan Uul in 1778AD [@bawden1989modern; @pozdneyev1971mongolia]. Ikh Khüree evolved from a tent monastery into the supreme demographic, theological and commercial metropolis of Outer Mongolia, housing monumental yellow-roofed temples, theological colleges (*datsan*), trade quarters (*Maimaicheng*) and international caravanserais, growing from 4,5k in 1650AD and 16k in 1778AD to 25k in 1820AD and 50k by 1911AD [@pozdneyev1971mongolia; @maiskii1921sovremennaya].

## The Dzungar-Khalkha Conflict and the 1691AD Dolon Nor Submission

In the late seventeenth century, the rise of the Dzungar Oirat Khanate under Galdan Boshugtu Khan precipitated catastrophic warfare across the steppe [@dicosmo1998qing; @bawden1989modern]. Territorial rivalries erupted into full-scale conflict in 1688AD when Galdan crossed the Khangai Mountains with thirty thousand Dzungar cavalry armed with muskets and camel-mounted artillery (*zamburak*), crushing the forces of Tüsheet Khan Chakhundorj, sacking Erdene Zuu and devastating monasteries throughout the Orkhon and Tuul valleys [@bawden1989modern; @atwood2004encyclopedia].

The invasion provoked mass displacement: hundreds of thousands of Khalkha nomads fled southward into the Gobi desert and Inner Mongolia under the leadership of Zanabazar and Chakhundorj [@bawden1989modern; @dicosmo1998qing]. Pastoral disruption, winter famine and epidemic mortality drove Khalkha population down from 580k in 1644AD to 560k around 1700AD, representing the lowest demographic benchmark of the modern era [@caoshuji2001zhongguo; @cao2024population].

Faced with annihilation by Galdan, the Khalkha leadership turned to the Qing Empire. In May 1691AD, the Kangxi Emperor convened the historic assembly of Dolon Nor (*Duolun*) in Inner Mongolia, where the Khalkha princes and Zanabazar formally swore fealty to the Qing crown [@dicosmo1998qing; @bawden1989modern]. In exchange for imperial military protection, which culminated in Qing victories over Galdan at Ulaan Butun (1690AD) and Zuunmod (1696AD), the Khalkha surrendered independent Chinggisid diplomatic autonomy and entered the Qing administrative orbit [@dicosmo1998qing; @caoshuji2001zhongguo].

## Qing Banner Administration and the Lifanyuan Governance Structure

Following Dolon Nor, the Qing Court of Colonial Affairs (*Lifanyuan*) reorganised Outer Mongolia into a rigid territorial banner (*khoshuu*) system designed to prevent inter-tribal coalition building and freeze nomadic mobility [@dicosmo1998qing; @caoshuji2001zhongguo]. The traditional three Khalkha aimags were sub-divided into thirty-four banners in 1691AD, proliferating through dynastic partitions to seventy-four banners by 1730AD and eighty-six banners by the nineteenth century [@bawden1989modern; @atwood2004encyclopedia].

In 1725AD, nineteen banners were detached from Tüsheet Khan aimag as a reward for Prince Tseren's loyalty during the Yongzheng reign, establishing the fourth Khalkha province: Sain Noyon Khan aimag in the Orkhon-Khangai highlands [@bawden1989modern; @caoshuji2001zhongguo]. Each banner was governed by an imperial jasag (*zasag*) sub-divided into military-fiscal units called *sumun* (formally containing 150 households), *arban* and *otog* [@dicosmo1998qing; @caoshuji2001zhongguo].

Qing military governance was anchored by the Military Governor of Uliastai (*Dingbian zuofujiangjun*), established in 1733AD in Zasagt Khan aimag to oversee defense against western Oirats and coordinate postal routes [@bawden1989modern; @caoshuji2001zhongguo]. Uliastai developed into a major fortified city with civilian suburbs, housing 8k inhabitants by 1820AD [@pozdneyev1971mongolia]. Further north, the Treaty of Kyakhta in 1727AD established the border trade depot of Altanbulag (Kyakhta Maimaicheng) opposite Russian Kyakhta, funneling lucrative tea, fur and textile caravans and supporting a resident commercial population of 8k by 1860AD [@pozdneyev1971mongolia; @maiskii1921sovremennaya].

## The Monastic Celibacy and Demographic Stagnation Debate

A central theme in modern Mongolian historiography is the demographic stagnation of the Qing era, where regional population expanded modestly from 560k in 1700AD to 644k in 1912AD (an annual growth rate of just 0,066%) [@caoshuji2001zhongguo; @bawden1989modern; @maiskii1921sovremennaya]. Scholars have long debated the relative contributions of monastic institutions, epidemic disease and pastoral economic constraints to this prolonged plateau [@caoshuji2001zhongguo; @Seddon2009Writings; @nrsaikhan2025Buddhist].

By the late nineteenth century, Russian surveys by Pozdneyev and Maiskii estimated that between 35% and 45% of the adult male population were ordained Buddhist lamas (*geleen* and *getshül*) bound to clerical celibacy [@pozdneyev1971mongolia; @maiskii1921sovremennaya]. In large monastic centres such as Ikh Khüree, Erdene Zuu, Amarbayasgalant and Zaya Gegeenii Khüree (Tsetserleg), thousands of young men resided permanently in temple dormitories, substantially depressing crude nuptiality and legitimate fertility rates [@bawden1989modern; @caoshuji2001zhongguo].

Furthermore, widespread venereal infections (particularly syphilis and gonorrhoea) introduced through seasonal Chinese merchant traffic and itinerant trading caravans contributed to high rates of primary and secondary sterility among pastoral women [@maiskii1921sovremennaya; @bawden1989modern]. Maiskii's medical surveys in 1919AD calculated that up to 50% of the adult population in urbanised trading centres suffered from venereal morbidity, leading to depressed birth rates and severe infant mortality [@maiskii1921sovremennaya].

Conversely, economic historians argue that monastic institutionalisation served vital welfare functions that cushioned nomadic pastoralism against environmental catastrophe [@Ujeed2015Establishment; @caoshuji2001zhongguo]. Monastic estates (*shabi*), administered directly by the Great Shabi office (*Ikh Shav*) on behalf of the Jebtsundamba Khutuktu, exempted herdsmen from Qing imperial corvée labor (*alba*) and military conscription [@bawden1989modern; @caoshuji2001zhongguo]. By 1911AD, the Jebtsundamba's shabi estates numbered over 18.000 households (roughly 90k persons), maintaining extensive emergency grain reserves and communal livestock lending systems that mitigated pastoral mortality during catastrophic winter freezes [@caoshuji2001zhongguo; @maiskii1921sovremennaya].

## The Khovd Ambanship, Western Frontier and 1911AD Independence

Western Mongolia followed a distinct administrative trajectory following the Qing destruction of the Dzungar state in 1757AD [@dicosmo1998qing; @bawden1989modern]. In 1761AD, the Qing court established an Imperial Residency (*Amban*) at Khovd (Kobdo) to govern the remaining Oirat populations (Dörbet, Zakhchin, Myangad, Ööld and Torguud banners) along with the Altai Uriankhai border guards [@caoshuji2001zhongguo; @atwood2004encyclopedia]. Khovd became the military and administrative bulwark of the western Altai frontier, protected by a fortified citadel (*Sangar*) and garrisoning Manchu, Mongol and Han military units alongside a thriving Chinese mercantile bazaar, reaching 6,8k inhabitants by 1820AD [@pozdneyev1971mongolia; @maiskii1921sovremennaya].

In eastern Mongolia, the imperial grazing lands of Dariganga were designated as specialized crown pastures under Lifanyuan supervision, breeding camels and horses for imperial courier posts and palaces [@caoshuji2001zhongguo]. In the north, the forested taiga around Lake Khövsgöl was garrisoned by Uriankhai and Darkhad border guards, preserving low population densities (0,2 persons per km²) adapted to reindeer herding and hunting [@caoshuji2001zhongguo; @maiskii1921sovremennaya].

At the opening of the twentieth century, late Qing implementation of the "New Policies" (*Xinzheng*) provoked severe unrest [@bawden1989modern; @Seddon2009Writings]. Beijing attempted to open Mongolian grasslands to Han agricultural colonisation, impose direct fiscal levies and establish colonial ministries, directly threatening nomadic pastoral territory and monastic estates [@bawden1989modern; @Teneg2024Reintroduction].

The outbreak of the Wuchang Uprising in China in October 1911 catalysed the Mongolian national independence movement [@bawden1989modern; @Mills2019Effects]. Led by Khalkha princes and high lamas, Mongol forces expelled the Qing Amban Sando from Ikh Khüree in December 1911. On 29 December 1911, the eighth Jebtsundamba Khutuktu was enthroned as the Bogd Khan (Holy Emperor) of independent Mongolia, establishing a theocratic monarchy [@bawden1989modern; @Mills2019Effects].

Subsequent military campaigns led by Magsarjav, Damdinsüren and Ja Lama liberated Uliastai and stormed the Qing fortress of Khovd in August 1912, eliminating imperial Chinese garrisons across the west and consolidating the sovereign boundary of the Bogd Khanate over 1,562M km² with 644k citizens [@bawden1989modern; @caoshuji2001zhongguo].

# Methodology

## Territorial Delimitation and Six-Aimag Administrative Partition

The spatial reconstruction encompasses 1.562.476 km² (26.461 five-arcminute grid cells) matching the sovereign territory of modern Mongolia and its historical nineteenth-century administrative predecessors. To maintain demographic continuity across seven centuries of changing provincial terminology, the territory is partitioned into six stable macro-units:

1. *Tüsheet Khan Aimag and Ikh Khüree*: Covering 405.246 km² (6.738 grid cells) in north-central Mongolia, spanning the central Tuul, Orkhon and Selenge river systems and containing the primary urban centres of Ulaanbaatar and Altanbulag.
2. *Setsen Khan Aimag*: Covering 321.224 km² (5.426 grid cells) across eastern Mongolia along the Kherlen and Onon river basins, including historical Avraga Ord, Choibalsan and Chinggis.
3. *Sain Noyon Khan Aimag*: Covering 236.703 km² (3.946 grid cells) in the central Khangai highlands, encompassing mediaeval Karakorum and nineteenth-century Tsetserleg.
4. *Zasagt Khan Aimag and Uliastai*: Covering 224.112 km² (3.766 grid cells) across western Khalkha territory, anchored by the Qing military governor's fortress at Uliastai.
5. *Khovd Frontier Ambanship*: Covering 186.737 km² (3.286 grid cells) across western Oirat territory, the Great Lakes Depression and the Mongolian Altai.
6. *Khövsgöl Uriankhai and Dariganga Banners*: Covering 188.454 km² (3.299 grid cells) comprising northern sub-arctic borderlands around Lake Khövsgöl and south-eastern imperial camel pastures in Dariganga.

## Household Multipliers and Banner Cadastral Synthesis

Demographic estimation across benchmark years $t \in [1206, 1912]$ integrates three distinct evidentiary corpora: mediaeval decimal troop levies, Qing banner household registers, and early twentieth-century census back-projections [@wusongdi2000zhongguo; @caoshuji2001zhongguo; @maiskii1921sovremennaya].

For the imperial era (1206AD to 1368AD), regional population $P_r(t)$ is derived from military *mingghan* registers and Yuan dynasty *hukou* returns synthesised by Wu Songdi [@wusongdi2000zhongguo; @allsen1987mongol]. Troop mobilisations were converted to total population using empirical pastoral household multipliers:

$$P_r(t) = M_r(t) \times \theta_p$$

where $M_r(t)$ denotes registered military levy capacity and $\theta_p = 7,0 \pm 0,5$ represents the total household multiplier, accounting for elderly dependents, women and children [@wusongdi2000zhongguo; @DR2019Modeling].

For the Qing era (1691AD to 1911AD), estimates draw on Shuji Cao's archival reconstructions of Lifanyuan banner registers (*khoshuu dan*), tribute rolls and shabi tax exemptions [@caoshuji2001zhongguo; @cao2024population]. Banner returns enumerating adult male subjects (*er*) were expanded using regional family structures, incorporating monastic populations enumerated in temple rolls [@caoshuji2001zhongguo; @pozdneyev1971mongolia]. Terminal benchmarks at 1911AD and 1912AD reconcile directly with Ivan Maiskii's comprehensive 1918–1919AD demographic survey of Outer Mongolia, which enumerated 647.500 indigenous Mongols across the Bogd Khanate [@maiskii1921sovremennaya; @bawden1989modern].

## Non-Stationary Matérn Kriging Calibration across East Asia

Spatial allocation within the six territorial masks draws upon the East Asian kriging calibration, which aggregates 87.810 radiocarbon, epigraphic and archaeological site-periods across 1.274 domestic Voronoi catchments (163.892 valid five-arcminute grid cells) plus 562 frontier conditioning catchments extending into Siberian Transbaikalia, northern China and Central Asia [@Wright2025Zuun; @Anon2021Study; @Kradin2018Heritage].

Following Freeman-Tukey square-root variance stabilisation and weighted least squares (WLS) regression on biophysical covariates (natural vegetation productivity, habitability fraction, terrain suitability, 13,5 km fluvial distance decay and smooth coastal proximity), residual spatial dependence is modelled with Paciorek-Schervish non-stationary Matérn ($\nu = 3/2$) covariance [@paciorek2006spatial]:

$$C(s_i, s_j) = \sigma_i \sigma_j \, |\Sigma_i|^{1/4} |\Sigma_j|^{1/4} \left|\frac{\Sigma_i + \Sigma_j}{2}\right|^{-1/2} \mathcal{M}_{3/2}\!\left(\sqrt{Q_{ij}}\right)$$

Across all ten Holocene horizons in the East Asian domain, regularised dimensionless variogram bandwidths stand at $\tau_1 = 1,50$ (raw 1,6277) and $\tau_2 = 2,775$, with an effective short range of 73,43 km, unregularised nugget-to-sill 0, regularised nugget-to-sill 0,04, and WLS goodness-of-fit $R^2 = 0,9995$ [@paciorek2006spatial]. Within each aimag mask, urban populations from 254 catalogued settlements are allocated directly to corresponding grid cells, with rural populations distributed across remaining habitable cells according to kriged pastoral potential surfaces [@Bemmann2020Karakorum; @S2026Spatial].

# Testing and Validation

Cross-checking provincial cadastral totals against Chinese, Russian and Mongolian primary sources confirms exact arithmetic consistency across all benchmark years from 1206AD to 1912AD. # Results

## Imperial Florescence and Yuan Expansion (1206 to 1368AD)

The unification of the steppe under Chinggis Khan initiated an era of rapid political concentration and demographic expansion (Figure \ref{fig:traj-mongol}). Aggregate numbers rose from 700k in 1206AD to 780k in 1290AD, reflecting the influx of tribute wealth, artisan imports and agricultural development in river valleys [@wusongdi2000zhongguo; @Bemmann2020Karakorum].

Tüsheet Khan aimag held the largest share of population, rising from 210k in 1206AD to 234k in 1290AD, followed by Setsen Khan aimag (133k rising to 148.200) and Sain Noyon Khan aimag (133k rising to 148.200) [@wusongdi2000zhongguo]. In the western territories, Zasagt Khan aimag expanded from 98k to 109.200, while the Khovd frontier district grew from 84k to 93.600 [@allsen1987mongol].

<figure class="crd-figure-block" id="fig:traj-mongol">
<img class="crd-figure-img" src="/artefacts/project_jade/1.0-mongol-empire-and-qing-mongolia/fig2_mongol_empire_and_qing_mongolia_trajectory.png" alt="fig:traj-mongol" loading="lazy" />
<figcaption class="crd-caption"><span class="crd-caption-label">Figure 2.</span> Population trajectory of Mongolia from 1206AD to 1912AD across six historical administrative territories with sub-regional trajectory bands.</figcaption>
</figure>

Urban development during this period was dominated by Karakorum in Sain Noyon Khan aimag (38k in 1255AD) and Avraga Ord in Setsen Khan aimag (14k in 1210AD) [@Bemmann2020Karakorum; @Wright2025Zuun]. These centres represented sophisticated administrative and industrial implants in a pastoral nomadic matrix, supported by royal storehouses and state-sponsored farming colonies [@Tolnai2026Tracing; @Vasyutin2026Origins].

## Post-Yuan Contraction and Steppe Reorganisation (1368 to 1691AD)

The collapse of the Yuan dynasty in 1368AD terminated imperial subsidies and triggered protracted civil conflict between eastern Chinggisid princes and western Oirat federations [@bawden1989modern; @cao2024population]. Total population contracted by 12,8% from 780k in 1290AD to 680k in 1368AD and reached a post-imperial trough of 580k by 1450AD (Figure \ref{fig:shares-mongol}).

<figure class="crd-figure-block" id="fig:shares-mongol">
<img class="crd-figure-img" src="/artefacts/project_jade/1.0-mongol-empire-and-qing-mongolia/fig3_mongol_empire_and_qing_mongolia_shares.png" alt="fig:shares-mongol" loading="lazy" />
<figcaption class="crd-caption"><span class="crd-caption-label">Figure 3.</span> Percentage demographic shares and benchmark population comparison across the six Mongolian territories between 1206AD and 1912AD.</figcaption>
</figure>

The sixteenth-century reunification under Dayan Khan provided temporary relief, expanding regional population back to 610k in 1550AD [@bawden1989modern]. However, the destructive Dzungar invasion led by Galdan Boshugtu Khan in 1688AD shattered Khalkha society, causing catastrophic losses in human lives and livestock herds that depressed the total to 560k by 1700AD [@dicosmo1998qing; @caoshuji2001zhongguo].

## Qing Era Stabilisation and Monastic Urbanism (1691 to 1912AD)

Following the 1691AD Dolon Nor submission, Qing imperial administration restructured Mongolia into static banners, eliminating inter-tribal warfare and establishing a stable legal order under the Lifanyuan [@dicosmo1998qing; @caoshuji2001zhongguo]. Population recovered gradually, climbing from 560k in 1700AD to 610k in 1776AD, 625k in 1820AD, 635k in 1851AD and 644k at independence in 1912AD (Table \ref{tab:regions-mongol}).

A defining feature of the Qing period was the growth of Buddhist monastic urbanism [@bawden1989modern; @pozdneyev1971mongolia]. Ikh Khüree (Urga) expanded into the uncontested primate metropolis of Mongolia, growing from 8,5k in 1700AD to 16k in 1778AD, 25k in 1820AD and 50k in 1911AD [@pozdneyev1971mongolia; @maiskii1921sovremennaya]. Other monastic and administrative centres developed into major regional hubs, including Uliastai (8k in 1820AD), Altanbulag (8k in 1860AD), Khovd (6,8k in 1820AD), Tsetserleg (5,5k in 1850AD), Choibalsan (5k in 1911AD), Chinggis (4,2k in 1911AD) and Amarbayasgalant (2,8k in 1820AD) [@pozdneyev1971mongolia; @maiskii1921sovremennaya].

# Limitations

Three principal historiographical and evidentiary constraints govern demographic precision across the 1206AD to 1912AD period. First, mediaeval decimal troop levies reflect military mobilisation capacity rather than direct headcounts [@allsen1987mongol; @wusongdi2000zhongguo]. While household multipliers of 6,5 to 7,5 persons per warrior are well grounded in comparative pastoral anthropology, they carry uncertainty intervals of approximately plus or minus 15% [@DR2019Modeling].

Second, Qing banner registers (*khoshuu dan*) primarily enumerated taxable adult males (*ding*) subject to corvée labor and military service, omitting women, infants and unordained youths [@caoshuji2001zhongguo; @bawden1989modern]. Furthermore, individuals registered under the Great Shabi estates were exempted from banner rolls and recorded separately in temple archives, necessitating careful institutional reconstruction to prevent undercounting [@caoshuji2001zhongguo; @Seddon2009Writings].

Third, spatial allocation across vast pastoral grasslands necessarily assumes smooth non-stationary density decays conditioned on environmental productivity and riverine proximity [@paciorek2006spatial; @Struck2022Central]. While urban centres such as Karakorum, Avraga, Ulaanbaatar and Uliastai are precisely located in the settlement gazetteer, purely nomadic encampments moved seasonally between pasture zones, so local micro-densities reflect pastoral carrying capacity rather than fixed residential permanence [@Honichud2022Mongolian; @S2026Spatial].

# Conclusion

Between 1206AD and 1912AD, Mongolia moved through a long cycle of imperial expansion, mediaeval urbanisation, post-Yuan political fragmentation and late-imperial monastic consolidation. The pastoral population expanded from 700k in 1206AD to 780k in 1290AD under the Pax Mongolica, when Karakorum and Avraga Ord flourished as cosmopolitan imperial capitals in an otherwise nomadic society. Following post-Yuan contraction and seventeenth-century devastation during the Dzungar wars, Qing banner administration stabilized regional boundaries, while the rise of Gelugpa monasticism fostered permanent urban growth centered on Ikh Khüree (50k in 1911AD).

By the declaration of national independence under the Bogd Khanate in 1912AD, Mongolia had restored its historical demographic equilibrium at 644k inhabitants across 1.562.476 km². Integrating primary Chinese cadastral returns, Russian geographical surveys and 254 catalogued settlements into the East Asian kriging domain establishes a coherent demographic baseline for twentieth-century modern state formation.
